docs.title: MorphLab
docs.text: MorphLab is an experimental software platform for developing, evaluating, and validating mechatronic mechanisms and control algorithms.

docs.title: Documentation
docs.text: The complete documentation is available through GitHub Pages.

docs.title: License
docs.text: MIT

docs.title: RFC-001: Platform Vision
docs.text: Field Value RFC RFC-001 Title Platform Vision Project MorphLab Status Draft Version 0.1 Author Mahdi Hooshmand Created YYYY-MM-DD

docs.title: 1. Abstract
docs.text:
This document defines the long-term vision, objectives, and guiding philosophy of the MorphLab platform.

MorphLab is a modular research platform intended to support the development, evaluation, and validation of mechatronic mechanisms, sensing systems, and control algorithms.

The platform is designed as a reusable research environment rather than software dedicated to a single mechanism or experiment.

docs.title: 2. Motivation
docs.text:
Research projects in mechatronics often require repeatedly implementing similar infrastructure for communication, control, data acquisition, visualization, logging, and analysis.

As hardware evolves, a significant portion of software is rewritten instead of reused.

MorphLab aims to separate reusable experimental infrastructure from hardware-specific implementations, allowing researchers to focus on scientific and engineering challenges instead of rebuilding supporting software.

docs.title: 3. Vision
docs.text:
The long-term vision of MorphLab is to become a unified experimental platform capable of supporting the complete lifecycle of mechatronic research.

The platform should provide a common environment for:

  • mechanism development
  • controller development
  • sensor integration
  • experiment execution
  • data acquisition
  • visualization
  • analysis
  • algorithm evaluation
  • reproducible research

In the long term, the platform should also provide the necessary foundation for Digital Twin technologies, enabling synchronization between physical systems and their virtual representations without requiring fundamental architectural changes.

docs.title: 4. Scope
docs.text:
MorphLab is intended for laboratory research, academic projects, and rapid prototyping.

Typical applications include:

  • Development of experimental mechanisms
  • Control algorithm research
  • Sensor evaluation
  • Kinematic analysis
  • Dynamic analysis
  • Calibration
  • Data acquisition
  • Data visualization
  • Experimental validation
  • Academic publications

docs.title: 5. Non-Goals
docs.text:
MorphLab is not intended to become:

  • An industrial automation framework
  • A PLC programming environment
  • A hard real-time operating system
  • A CAD system
  • A physics simulation engine
  • A commercial robotics framework

Integration with such systems may be supported in future versions.

docs.title: Research First
docs.text:
The platform exists to accelerate scientific research.

Architectural decisions should prioritize flexibility, extensibility, and observability over optimization for a single application.

docs.title: Experiment-Centric
docs.text:
Experiments are the primary unit of work.

Mechanisms, sensors, controllers, algorithms, and visualization tools exist to support experimental workflows.

docs.title: Hardware Independence
docs.text:
The platform should minimize dependency on specific hardware.

Controllers, communication methods, sensors, and computing devices are expected to evolve independently.

docs.title: Mechanism Independence
docs.text:
No mechanism should receive special treatment.

Each mechanism should integrate into the platform through common abstractions.

docs.title: Extensibility
docs.text: Future capabilities should be added with minimal modification to existing components.

docs.title: Reproducibility
docs.text: Experimental configurations, acquired data, algorithms, and metadata should be preserved to enable reproducible research.

docs.title: Separation of Concerns
docs.text: Communication, control, visualization, analysis, logging, and hardware integration should remain independent responsibilities.

docs.title: 7. Long-Term Objectives
docs.text:
MorphLab should gradually evolve toward supporting:

  • Multiple experimental mechanisms
  • Multiple controller architectures
  • Multiple sensor systems
  • Distributed computing
  • Remote experimentation
  • Digital Twin integration
  • Hardware-in-the-loop experiments
  • Software-in-the-loop experiments
  • Automated experiment pipelines

docs.title: 8. Out of Scope
docs.text:
This RFC intentionally does not define:

  • Software architecture
  • Runtime architecture
  • Programming languages
  • APIs
  • Communication protocols
  • Hardware platforms
  • File formats
  • Internal modules

These subjects are specified by subsequent RFCs, ADRs, Standards, and Specifications.

docs.title: 9. Summary
docs.text:
MorphLab is intended to become a reusable research platform for experimental mechatronics.

Individual mechanisms, controllers, sensors, and experimental setups are expected to evolve continuously.

The platform itself should remain stable, extensible, and reusable across these changes.

docs.title: RFC-002: Terminology
docs.text: Field Value RFC RFC-002 Title Terminology Project MorphLab Status Draft Version 0.1 Author Mahdi Hooshmand Created YYYY-MM-DD

docs.title: 1. Abstract
docs.text:
This document defines the official terminology used throughout the MorphLab project.

The purpose of this RFC is to establish a common vocabulary for documentation, software architecture, implementation, and future research.

Unless explicitly stated otherwise, all subsequent RFCs, ADRs, Standards, and Specifications shall use the terminology defined in this document.

docs.title: 2. Platform
docs.text:
The complete software environment that supports the development, execution, monitoring, recording, and analysis of experiments.

The Platform represents the entire MorphLab ecosystem.

docs.title: 3. Experiment
docs.text:
The primary research entity within MorphLab.

An Experiment represents a reproducible scientific investigation conducted to evaluate one or more hypotheses.

An Experiment defines the context in which research activities are performed.

The conceptual composition of an Experiment is defined in RFC-003 (Domain Model).

docs.title: 4. Mechanism
docs.text:
A physical or virtual mechanical system under investigation.

A Mechanism may contain moving structures, joints, transmissions, or any other mechanical elements.

A Mechanism does not include controllers or software.

Examples:

  • Three-axis experimental platform
  • Robotic arm
  • Stewart platform
  • Gimbal
  • Inverted pendulum

docs.title: 5. Device
docs.text:
Any hardware component capable of interacting with the platform.

Devices may provide sensing, actuation, communication, computation, or auxiliary functionality.

Examples:

  • Microcontroller
  • IMU
  • Motor Driver
  • Camera
  • Mobile Phone
  • Force Sensor

docs.title: 6. Controller
docs.text:
A Device responsible for executing low-level control logic and directly interacting with hardware.

Typical responsibilities include:

  • Reading sensors
  • Driving actuators
  • Executing deterministic control loops
  • Reporting measurements

A Controller does not perform high-level experiment management.

docs.title: 7. Sensor
docs.text:
A Device that measures physical quantities.

Examples include:

  • Encoder
  • Potentiometer
  • IMU
  • Camera
  • Force Sensor
  • Temperature Sensor

Sensors generate observations but do not modify the physical system.

docs.title: 8. Actuator
docs.text:
A Device capable of modifying the physical state of a mechanism.

Examples include:

  • DC Motor
  • Stepper Motor
  • Servo Motor
  • Hydraulic Actuator
  • Pneumatic Cylinder

docs.title: 9. Data Source
docs.text:
Any provider of observable data.

A Data Source may be:

  • Physical Sensor
  • Software Module
  • External Application
  • Simulation
  • Remote System

Every Sensor is a Data Source.

Not every Data Source is a Sensor.

docs.title: 10. Observation
docs.text:
A single measured value produced by a Data Source.

Examples:

  • Position
  • Velocity
  • Roll
  • Pitch
  • Yaw
  • Acceleration
  • Angular Velocity

Observations always represent measurements.

docs.title: 11. State
docs.text:
A collection of observations describing the current condition of a system at a particular instant.

State represents the best available knowledge about the system.

State may contain measured, estimated, or calculated values.

docs.title: 12. Control Algorithm
docs.text:
An algorithm responsible for determining actuator commands based on available state information.

Examples:

  • PID
  • LQR
  • MPC
  • Adaptive Control
  • Reinforcement Learning

The platform imposes no restrictions on algorithm implementation.

docs.title: 13. Command
docs.text:
A requested action issued to a Device or Controller.

Examples include:

  • Set Motor Velocity
  • Set Position
  • Enable Output
  • Disable Output

Commands describe desired behavior rather than measured state.

docs.title: 14. Session
docs.text:
A continuous period during which the platform operates.

A Session may contain one or more Experiments.

docs.title: 15. Dataset
docs.text:
A structured collection of recorded experimental data.

Datasets may contain:

  • Measurements
  • Commands
  • Events
  • Metadata
  • Configuration

Datasets are intended for offline analysis and publication.

docs.title: 16. Logger
docs.text:
A software component responsible for recording information generated during a Session or Experiment.

Logging is independent of analysis.

docs.title: 17. Analysis
docs.text:
The process of extracting information from experimental data.

Analysis may include:

  • Statistical processing
  • Error estimation
  • Performance evaluation
  • Model validation
  • Visualization

Analysis does not modify recorded data.

docs.title: 18. Visualization
docs.text:
The graphical presentation of experimental information.

Visualization may include:

  • Live monitoring
  • Charts
  • Time-series plots
  • Three-dimensional views
  • Dashboards

Visualization is independent of data acquisition.

docs.title: 19. Configuration
docs.text:
A collection of parameters describing how an Experiment is executed.

Configuration may include:

  • Hardware selection
  • Control parameters
  • Sampling rates
  • Calibration values
  • Experiment settings

Configuration should be reproducible.

docs.title: 20. Digital Twin
docs.text:
A virtual representation of a physical system synchronized with experimental data.

Digital Twin support is considered a long-term capability of MorphLab and is outside the scope of the initial implementation.

docs.title: 21. Simulation
docs.text:
A computational model that emulates the behavior of a mechanism or subsystem.

Simulation may replace physical hardware during development or validation.

Simulation is not required for every Experiment.

docs.title: 22. Plugin
docs.text:
A software component that extends the platform without modifying its core.

Plugins may introduce:

  • Devices
  • Mechanisms
  • Visualizations
  • Analysis tools
  • Communication interfaces

docs.title: 23. Future Terms
docs.text: Additional terminology shall be introduced only through new RFCs or revisions to this document.

docs.title: 24. Summary
docs.text:
The terminology defined in this RFC establishes the common language of MorphLab.

Future documentation and software should consistently use these definitions to ensure architectural clarity and long-term maintainability.

docs.title: Relationship to Other RFCs
docs.text:
This document defines the official terminology of MorphLab.

Definitions provided here intentionally avoid describing relationships between entities.

The conceptual relationships between these terms are specified in RFC-003 (Domain Model).

docs.title: RFC-003: Domain Model
docs.text: Field Value RFC RFC-003 Title Domain Model Project MorphLab Status Draft Version 0.1 Author Mahdi Hooshmand Created YYYY-MM-DD

docs.title: 1. Abstract
docs.text:
This document defines the conceptual domain model of MorphLab.

The purpose of this RFC is to describe the primary domain entities and their relationships.

Implementation details, software architecture, APIs, communication protocols, and programming languages are intentionally excluded.

Definitions of individual terms are provided in RFC-002 (Terminology).

docs.title: 2. Purpose
docs.text:
MorphLab is intended to support a wide variety of experimental workflows.

To ensure long-term consistency, the platform is built upon a stable conceptual domain model independent of implementation technologies.

This RFC specifies that conceptual model.

docs.title: 3. Domain Model
docs.text:
The conceptual domain model consists of the following entities.

  • Experiment
  • Mechanism
  • Device
  • Controller
  • Sensor
  • Actuator
  • Data Source
  • Observation
  • State
  • Control Algorithm
  • Command
  • Dataset
  • Logger
  • Analysis
  • Visualization
  • Configuration
  • Session
  • Plugin
  • Simulation
  • Digital Twin

The definitions of these entities are provided in RFC-002.

docs.title: Experiment
docs.text:
An Experiment:

  • investigates one or more hypotheses
  • uses one Mechanism
  • uses one or more Control Algorithms
  • acquires data from one or more Data Sources
  • issues Commands
  • records one or more Datasets
  • performs Analysis
  • produces Results

docs.title: Mechanism
docs.text:
A Mechanism:

  • contains physical components
  • is observed by Sensors
  • is influenced by Actuators
  • is controlled through one or more Controllers

docs.title: Controller
docs.text:
A Controller:

  • communicates with Devices
  • acquires Sensor observations
  • issues Commands to Actuators
  • exchanges information with the Platform

docs.title: Sensor
docs.text:
A Sensor:

  • is a Device
  • is a Data Source
  • produces Observations

docs.title: Actuator
docs.text:
An Actuator:

  • is a Device
  • receives Commands
  • modifies the physical state of a Mechanism

docs.title: Observation
docs.text:
Observations:

  • originate from Data Sources
  • contribute to State estimation
  • may be recorded within Datasets

docs.title: State
docs.text:
State:

  • represents the current condition of the system
  • is composed of one or more Observations
  • may include estimated values

docs.title: Control Algorithm
docs.text:
A Control Algorithm:

  • receives State information
  • produces Commands
  • may be evaluated against other algorithms

docs.title: Dataset
docs.text:
A Dataset:

  • belongs to an Experiment
  • contains Observations
  • may contain Commands
  • may contain Events
  • includes Metadata

docs.title: Analysis
docs.text:
Analysis:

  • consumes Datasets
  • produces evaluation metrics
  • generates derived information

docs.title: Visualization
docs.text:
Visualization:

  • presents information to users
  • may consume live or recorded data

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Configuration:

  • belongs to an Experiment
  • defines execution parameters
  • supports reproducibility

docs.title: Session
docs.text:
A Session:

  • contains one or more Experiments
  • represents a continuous execution period

docs.title: Plugin
docs.text:
A Plugin:

  • extends platform capabilities
  • may introduce new Devices
  • may introduce new Mechanisms
  • may introduce Analysis or Visualization components

docs.title: Simulation
docs.text:
Simulation:

  • represents a virtual implementation of a Mechanism
  • may replace physical hardware during an Experiment

docs.title: Digital Twin
docs.text:
A Digital Twin:

  • represents a synchronized virtual representation of a physical system
  • may consume live observations
  • is considered an optional future capability

docs.title: 5. Conceptual View
docs.text:
Experiment
│
├── Configuration
├── Mechanism
│   ├── Sensor(s)
│   ├── Actuator(s)
│   └── Controller(s)
│
├── Control Algorithm(s)
├── Data Source(s)
├── Observation(s)
├── State
├── Dataset(s)
├── Analysis
├── Visualization
└── Results

This diagram illustrates conceptual ownership only.

It does not define software modules or runtime architecture.

docs.title: 6. Architectural Independence
docs.text:
The Domain Model is independent of:

  • Programming languages
  • Operating systems
  • Communication protocols
  • Runtime architecture
  • Software modules
  • Hardware platforms

Future implementation technologies shall preserve this conceptual model whenever practical.

docs.title: 7. Extensibility
docs.text:
Additional domain entities may be introduced in future RFC revisions.

Existing entities should remain stable to preserve compatibility across the MorphLab ecosystem.

docs.title: 8. Summary
docs.text:
The Domain Model provides the conceptual foundation of MorphLab.

Subsequent RFCs, ADRs, Standards, and Specifications shall build upon the relationships defined in this document.

docs.title: RFC-004: System Context
docs.text: Field Value RFC RFC-004 Title System Context Project MorphLab Status Draft Version 0.1 Author Mahdi Hooshmand Created YYYY-MM-DD

docs.title: 1. Abstract
docs.text:
This document defines the system boundary of MorphLab and identifies the external actors and systems that interact with the platform.

The purpose of this RFC is to establish a common understanding of what belongs to MorphLab and what remains outside its responsibility.

This document intentionally avoids software architecture and implementation details.

docs.title: 2. Purpose
docs.text:
MorphLab operates as the central software platform for experimental mechatronics research.

The platform coordinates experiments, communicates with external systems, collects observations, executes analysis workflows, and manages experimental data.

External hardware and software systems interact with MorphLab through well-defined interfaces.

docs.title: 3. System Boundary
docs.text:
MorphLab is responsible for:

  • Experiment management
  • Configuration management
  • Device integration
  • Data acquisition
  • State management
  • Data synchronization
  • Data logging
  • Analysis
  • Visualization
  • Experiment evaluation
  • Result generation

MorphLab is not responsible for implementing hardware devices, operating systems, embedded firmware, or external software tools.

docs.title: Researcher
docs.text:
The primary user of MorphLab.

Responsibilities include:

  • Designing experiments
  • Configuring experiments
  • Executing experiments
  • Monitoring execution
  • Evaluating results

docs.title: Physical Mechanism
docs.text:
The mechanical system being investigated.

The mechanism is external to MorphLab.

MorphLab observes and controls the mechanism but does not define its mechanical design.

docs.title: Controllers
docs.text:
Embedded control hardware responsible for low-level interaction with mechanisms.

Controllers execute hardware-specific logic and exchange information with MorphLab.

Controllers remain external systems.

docs.title: Measurement Systems
docs.text:
Independent systems that provide experimental observations.

Examples include:

  • IMUs
  • Motion capture systems
  • Optical tracking systems
  • Mobile devices
  • External sensors

MorphLab treats all measurement systems as external observation providers.

docs.title: Visualization Clients
docs.text:
External applications used to visualize experimental information.

Examples may include desktop applications, web applications, or mobile interfaces.

Visualization clients consume information generated by MorphLab.

docs.title: Data Consumers
docs.text:
External software responsible for post-processing experimental data.

Examples include:

  • Scientific computing environments
  • Machine learning frameworks
  • Statistical analysis tools
  • Publication pipelines

MorphLab provides data but does not control downstream analysis tools.

docs.title: 5. External Systems
docs.text:
The following systems are considered external to MorphLab.

  • Embedded firmware
  • Hardware drivers
  • Operating systems
  • Network infrastructure
  • Storage infrastructure
  • Simulation software
  • CAD software
  • Numerical solvers
  • Scientific software packages

MorphLab may integrate with these systems without becoming dependent on them.

docs.title: 6. High-Level Context
docs.text:
+----------------------+
                   |      Researcher      |
                   +----------+-----------+
                              |
                              |
                              v
                 +--------------------------+
                 |         MorphLab         |
                 +--------------------------+
                  |      |        |       |
                  |      |        |       |
                  v      v        v       v
          Controllers  Measurement  Visualization
             |          Systems        Clients
             |              |
             +------+-------+
                    |
                    v
             Physical Mechanism

                    |
                    v

             Experimental Data

                    |
                    v

              External Analysis

This diagram illustrates conceptual interactions only.

It does not represent software architecture or runtime communication.

docs.title: 7. Responsibility Model
docs.text:
MorphLab owns:

  • Experimental workflows
  • Experimental data
  • Experimental metadata
  • Data synchronization
  • Analysis workflows
  • Result generation

External systems own:

  • Hardware implementation
  • Firmware implementation
  • Physical sensing
  • Physical actuation
  • Mechanical behavior
  • Operating system services

docs.title: 8. Design Implications
docs.text:
The system boundary establishes several architectural consequences.

  • External hardware shall be replaceable.

  • Multiple hardware implementations may coexist.

  • Multiple measurement systems may observe the same mechanism.

  • Multiple visualization clients may consume the same experimental data.

  • Experimental workflows shall remain independent from specific hardware implementations.

docs.title: 9. Future Extensions
docs.text:
The defined system boundary supports future integration of additional external systems, including:

  • Digital Twin platforms
  • Hardware-in-the-loop systems
  • Software-in-the-loop systems
  • Cloud-based execution environments
  • Distributed experiments
  • Autonomous data analysis systems

These additions should not require redefining the MorphLab system boundary.

docs.title: 10. Summary
docs.text:
MorphLab acts as the central orchestration platform for experimental research.

It coordinates experiments and manages scientific workflows while remaining independent from specific hardware, firmware, operating systems, and external software tools.

The system boundary defined in this RFC serves as the foundation for subsequent architectural decisions.

docs.title: RFC-005: Design Principles
docs.text: Field Value RFC RFC-005 Title Design Principles Project MorphLab Status Draft Version 0.1 Author Mahdi Hooshmand Created YYYY-MM-DD

docs.title: 1. Abstract
docs.text:
This document defines the fundamental design principles governing the evolution of MorphLab.

These principles provide the foundation for future architectural decisions, implementation strategies, Standards, and ADRs.

All future design decisions should comply with these principles unless an ADR explicitly justifies an exception.

docs.title: 2. Purpose
docs.text:
MorphLab is intended to remain a reusable experimental platform over many years of research.

To achieve this goal, software architecture shall be guided by stable engineering principles rather than implementation-specific decisions.

docs.title: 3.1 Research First
docs.text:
MorphLab exists to accelerate scientific research.

Engineering decisions shall prioritize flexibility, repeatability, and observability over premature optimization.

docs.title: 3.2 Experiment-Centric Design
docs.text:
The primary unit of work is an Experiment.

All platform capabilities ultimately exist to support the planning, execution, observation, analysis, and evaluation of experiments.

docs.title: 3.3 Scientific Reproducibility
docs.text:
Experimental results should be reproducible.

An Experiment should contain sufficient information to allow another researcher to reproduce the workflow and evaluate the results.

docs.title: 3.4 Long-Term Evolution
docs.text:
The platform is expected to evolve continuously.

New mechanisms, devices, algorithms, and technologies should be integrated without redesigning the conceptual model.

docs.title: 4.1 Separation of Concerns
docs.text:
Each software component should have a single well-defined responsibility.

Communication, data acquisition, experiment execution, visualization, logging, and analysis shall remain independent concerns.

docs.title: 4.2 Hardware Independence
docs.text:
Core platform functionality shall remain independent of specific hardware implementations.

Replacing a controller, sensor, actuator, or computing device should require minimal changes outside the corresponding integration layer.

docs.title: 4.3 Transport Independence
docs.text:
Communication mechanisms are implementation details.

The platform shall not depend on a particular transport technology such as Serial, TCP, UDP, USB, Bluetooth, or Wi-Fi.

docs.title: 4.4 Device Abstraction
docs.text:
The platform shall interact with capabilities rather than hardware implementations.

Device-specific behavior should remain isolated behind well-defined abstractions.

docs.title: 4.5 Extensibility
docs.text:
New functionality should be introduced by extension rather than modification whenever practical.

Adding support for new mechanisms or devices should minimize changes to existing software.

docs.title: 4.6 Data-Centric Architecture
docs.text:
Experimental data is a primary asset of the platform.

Software components should exchange structured data rather than implementation-specific objects whenever practical.

docs.title: 4.7 Time-Aware Data
docs.text:
Experimental observations should preserve temporal information.

Whenever possible, recorded observations should include timestamps to enable synchronization, replay, and analysis.

docs.title: 4.8 Deterministic Logging
docs.text:
Information produced during an Experiment should be recordable.

Logging should not depend on the execution mode or visualization tools.

docs.title: 4.9 Analysis Independence
docs.text:
Analysis shall operate on recorded experimental data rather than requiring direct hardware access.

Offline analysis should be equivalent, whenever practical, to online analysis.

docs.title: 4.10 Visualization Independence
docs.text:
Visualization is a consumer of information, not a producer.

Experimental workflows shall not depend on a particular visualization technology.

docs.title: 4.11 Configuration as Data
docs.text:
Experimental configuration should be represented as structured data.

Configurations should be portable, versionable, and reproducible.

docs.title: 4.12 Progressive Fidelity
docs.text:
The platform shall support gradual improvements in hardware quality.

Higher-quality sensors, more accurate actuators, Digital Twins, simulations, or additional measurement systems should improve experimental accuracy without requiring redesign of the platform.

docs.title: 4.13 Reference-Based Validation
docs.text:
Whenever available, independent reference measurements should be usable for validation, calibration, and performance evaluation.

The platform shall treat reference measurements as first-class experimental data.

docs.title: 4.14 Technology Neutrality
docs.text:
Programming languages, operating systems, communication protocols, and embedded platforms are implementation choices.

No implementation technology shall become part of the conceptual architecture.

docs.title: 5. Architectural Implications
docs.text:
Future architectural decisions should preserve these principles.

When trade-offs become necessary, ADRs shall explicitly identify:

  • Which principles are affected.
  • Why the trade-off is necessary.
  • How the long-term impact is mitigated.

docs.title: 6. Future Evolution
docs.text:
These principles are expected to remain stable throughout the lifetime of MorphLab.

New capabilities should extend these principles rather than replace them.

docs.title: 7. Summary
docs.text:
The Design Principles defined in this RFC establish the engineering philosophy of MorphLab.

They provide a stable foundation for future architecture, implementation, and long-term evolution while remaining independent of specific technologies.
